## Available skills

Skills are packaged instructions for specific kinds of tasks. The following skills are available:

- circleci-builds: Diagnose and fix failing CircleCI builds quickly and safely. Use when users ask to investigate failed CircleCI jobs, triage flaky pipelines, identify root causes from logs, and implement minimal fixes in configuration, test setup, or build-related code paths.
- circleci-cli: Day-to-day CircleCI from the terminal with the circleci CLI — authenticate, validate config before you commit, watch the run your push triggered, review pipeline/workflow/job status, print a failure report for your latest failed run in one command, read job logs and failed tests, list a project's flaky tests, list or download every artifact in a run in one command, and rerun/cancel/trigger. Use when a developer asks to authenticate CLI access, check their build or pipeline status, watch a run after pushing, see why CI failed, read job output/logs, find failing tests, list flaky tests, download build outputs such as a coverage report, rerun failed jobs, cancel or re-trigger a run, validate a config change locally, or look up a project's environment variables, contexts, triggers or pipeline definitions. For first-time project connection / pipeline-definition setup use the onboarding skill; for the diagnose-and-fix methodology on a failing build use circleci-builds.
- circleci-config: Optimize CircleCI configuration for speed, reliability, and maintainability. Use when users ask to improve `.circleci/config.yml`, reduce CI runtime, tune caching/workspaces/parallelism, remove pipeline waste, or fix flaky pipeline behavior caused by configuration choices.
- circleci-deploy-setup: Set up, audit, or regenerate CircleCI deploy markers, deploy and rollback pipelines, and release validation in a repository. Use when a user wants to onboard a project to deploys, releases, deploy markers, smart deployments, release validation or auto-rollback; when they ask what deploy setup a repo already has or whether it is complete; when they want to regenerate or upgrade an existing deploy.yml, rollback.yml, or marker setup; or when they ask to replicate the Deploys setup wizard locally. Covers config generation, verification, pipeline registration, and wiring validation webhooks from Datadog, Grafana, Prometheus, Alertmanager, or any tool that can POST to a URL. For first-time project connection and basic pipeline setup use the onboarding skill.
- circleci-smarter-testing-debugging: Debug CircleCI Smarter Testing on a project that is already onboarded, using `circleci testsuite impact` to explore impact data (which files impact a test, which tests a file impacts) and `circleci testsuite result` to show how a job's test atoms were selected and how they ran. Use when asking why a test was selected or skipped, why a change didn't run the expected tests, why too many tests run, or how a test atom ran in a job. For first-time setup use circleci-smarter-testing-onboarding.
- circleci-smarter-testing-onboarding: Onboard a project onto CircleCI Smarter Testing — check the default suite for the detected test runner (or write `.circleci/test-suites.yml` when it doesn't fit), replace the raw test step (or legacy `circleci tests glob`/`split`/`run`) with `circleci testsuite run`, validate with `circleci testsuite doctor`, make sure the free features work (static test splitting, rerun only failed tests, test uploads), then ask if any credit-charged features should be enabled (test impact analysis, dynamic test splitting, dynamic parallelism, auto rerun failed tests). Use for first-time setup of Smarter Testing, testsuite, test-suites YAML, or migrating a test step. Not for running (circleci-smarter-testing-run) or debugging a suite that is already onboarded.
- circleci-smarter-testing-run: Run a project's tests locally through CircleCI Smarter Testing with `circleci testsuite run`, which detects the test runner when there is no `.circleci/test-suites.yml`, narrowed to a subset with `--test-atom-pattern`, instead of calling the test runner directly. Use whenever you are about to run tests (`go test`, `npm test`, `pytest`, `jest`, `vitest`, `rspec`, `gradle test` and so on) in a repository that has `.circleci/test-suites.yml` or `.circleci/config.yml`, including running one package, file or directory of tests while iterating. For first-time setup use circleci-smarter-testing-onboarding; for why a test was selected or skipped use circleci-smarter-testing-debugging.
- debug-ci-failures: Debug CircleCI build failures, analyze test results, and identify flaky tests. Use when the user says "debug CI", "why is CI failing", "fix CI failures", "find flaky tests", "what broke in CI", "check CircleCI", or asks about failing pipelines or build errors.
- onboarding: Agent-driven onboarding guide for CircleCI. Walks a user through the full setup journey: account creation, organization selection or creation, GitHub App connection, project creation, pipeline definition + trigger, and iterating a config file until it passes. Everything is done from the terminal with the circleci CLI — never send the user to the web app for something a command can do. Use this skill whenever a user says "onboard to CircleCI", "set up CircleCI", "get started with CircleCI", "connect my repo to CircleCI", "create a CircleCI project", or asks for help with any early CircleCI setup step. Also trigger if the user has a new repo and wants CI running on it. For day-to-day work on an already-connected project (watch a run, read failing logs, rerun) use the circleci-cli skill instead.

# Skill: circleci-config

# CircleCI Config

## Overview

Use this skill to improve CircleCI performance and stability without changing product behavior. Focus on measured bottlenecks first, then implement the smallest safe config changes with clear validation criteria.

Read `references/cache-optimization.md` when the request involves `save_cache`, `restore_cache`, `persist_to_workspace`, `attach_workspace`, cache key design, dependency caching, lockfiles, or complaints about low cache hit rates, oversized caches, or wasted persistence steps.
Read `references/persisting-data.md` when the request involves choosing between caches, workspaces, and artifacts, or when data is being moved between jobs inefficiently.
Read `references/test-results.md` when the request involves slow test jobs, parallelism, tests timings, or missing JUnit XML.
Read `references/patterns.md` when the request involves approvals, branch/tag filters, schedules, deploy flow structure, or environment promotion patterns.

## Inputs To Gather

- `.yaml` and `.yml` files in `.circleci/` and any reusable config fragments
- Current pain points: duration, flakiness, cost, or maintainability
- Baseline metrics: slowest jobs, most frequent retries/failures, queue and run times
- Risk tolerance for structural changes

## Workflow

1. Build a baseline.
   - Identify top 1-3 longest jobs and top flaky jobs.
   - Capture before metrics (duration, pass rate, retries).
2. Remove pipeline waste.
   - Eliminate duplicate jobs/workflows.
   - Tighten branch/tag filters and workflow triggers.
3. Improve dependency and artifact flow.
   - Fix cache keys to include deterministic lockfile checks.
   - Use workspaces/artifacts to avoid rebuilding identical outputs.
   - Prefer cache scopes that are narrow, reproducible, and cheap to restore.
4. Apply safe parallelism.
   - Parallelize only proven bottlenecks.
   - Keep fan-out/fan-in readable and deterministic.
5. Validate impact.
   - Define expected metric changes and acceptance criteria before finalizing.

## Guardrails

- Prefer configuration fixes before proposing application code changes.
- When adding a new job or setup step, check `circleci function list` (or `list_functions`) first. Don't move a working pipeline's orbs to Functions unless the user asks.
- Do not add blanket retries to hide deterministic failures.
- Preserve deployment safety gates while optimizing build/test stages.
- Keep changes incremental and easy to revert.
- Prefer language-specific cache directories over broad project snapshots.
- Avoid cache keys that rotate every run unless the user explicitly wants effectively write-only caches.

## Output Contract

Provide:

1. Baseline bottleneck summary.
2. Proposed or applied config changes with rationale.
3. Expected runtime/reliability impact.
4. Validation plan and rollback note.

---
Bundled files (read with read_skill_file):
- references/cache-optimization.md
- references/patterns.md
- references/persisting-data.md
- references/test-results.md

version: 2.1

functions:
  setup-go: github.com/circleci-functions/setup-go@v0.6.0

commands:
  setup:
    steps:
      - checkout
      - install-go
      - install-task

  # Installs the toolchain and restores the module, build and lint caches, saved at job end.
  install-go:
    steps:
      - setup-go:
          with:
            version-file: go.mod
            golangci-lint-cache: true
            checksum: '{{ checksum "go.sum" }}_{{ checksum "clikit/go.sum" }}_{{ checksum "tools/go.sum" }}'
      - run: go version

  install-task:
    steps:
      - run:
          name: Install go-task
          command: |
            sh -c "$(curl --location https://taskfile.dev/install.sh)" -- -d -b "$HOME/.local/bin"
            echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> "$BASH_ENV"

  # GoReleaser's dockers_v2 pipe shells out to `docker buildx build`, so the
  # builder and the registry login have to exist before it runs.
  setup-docker:
    steps:
      - run:
          name: Register QEMU for cross-architecture builds
          # Dockerfile.alpine RUNs `apk add`, once per platform in the manifest,
          # so building its arm64 half on an amd64 host needs binfmt handlers
          # registered. Idempotent, and a no-op for the cimg/base image, which
          # only COPYs.
          command: docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install arm64
      - run:
          name: Create a buildx builder
          # The machine image's default buildx driver is `docker`, which can
          # neither build for two platforms in one invocation nor push a
          # manifest list. A docker-container driver can do both.
          command: docker buildx create --use --driver docker-container
      - run:
          name: Log in to Docker Hub
          # Absent on branch dry-runs, which have no context: the snapshot build
          # still exercises the Dockerfile, it just pushes nothing.
          command: |
            if [ -z "${DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME:-}" ]; then
              echo "No Docker Hub credentials — skipping login (snapshot builds do not push)."
              exit 0
            fi
            echo "$DOCKER_HUB_PASSWORD" | docker login --username "$DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME" --password-stdin

  store_results:
    steps:
      - store_test_results:
          path: ./test-reports

executors:
  linux:
    machine:
      image: ubuntu-2604:current
    resource_class: large.gen3

  # Arm64 counterpart to `linux`, for checking both halves of a multi-arch
  # image. Deliberately small: it only pulls and runs a container.
  linux-arm:
    machine:
      image: ubuntu-2604:current
    resource_class: arm.medium

  macos:
    macos:
      xcode: 26.5.0

  windows:
    machine: true
    resource_class: windows.medium

jobs:
  check:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - setup
      - run: task ci:check
      - store_results

  test:
    parameters:
      executor:
        type: executor
    executor: << parameters.executor >>
    steps:
      - setup
      - run: task ci:test
      - store_results

  deploy:
    executor: linux
    parameters:
      # Run before anything is installed, so a push with nothing to release
      # stops cheaply.
      gate_steps:
        type: steps
        default: []
      publish_steps:
        type: steps
        default:
          - run: task ci:release
    steps:
      - setup
      - steps: << parameters.gate_steps >>
      - setup-docker
      - run: sudo apt update --yes
      - run:
          name: Install snapcraft
          command: |
            sudo apt install snapd --yes
            sudo snap install snapcraft --classic
      - run:
          name: Install choco
          command: |
            sudo cp tools/choco.sh /usr/local/bin/choco
            sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/choco
            choco help
      - steps: << parameters.publish_steps >>
      - store_artifacts:
          path: dist

  smoke-test:
    parameters:
      executor:
        type: executor
      install-steps:
        type: steps
    executor: << parameters.executor >>
    steps:
      - steps: << parameters.install-steps >>
      - run:
          name: Verify circleci binary
          command: circleci version

  # Matrixed over the executors rather than over the tags: only the architecture
  # needs a machine of its own, so each job checks both variants. Printing the
  # arch inside the container makes the log say which half of the manifest ran. A
  # tag missing this platform fails here anyway — the arm machine images carry no
  # binfmt, so there is nothing to silently emulate an amd64-only image with.
  smoke-test-docker:
    parameters:
      executor:
        type: executor
    executor: << parameters.executor >>
    steps:
      - run:
          name: Verify circleci/circleci-cli:v1
          command: docker run --rm circleci/circleci-cli:v1 sh -c 'uname -m; circleci version'
      - run:
          name: Verify circleci/circleci-cli:v1-alpine
          command: docker run --rm circleci/circleci-cli:v1-alpine sh -c 'uname -m; circleci version'

  # Opens or updates the release PR (see RELEASE.md).
  release-pr:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - setup
      - run: task ci:release-pr

  docs:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - setup
      - run:
          name: Generate reference and build the site
          command: task docs:build
      - run:
          name: Check internal links
          command: task docs:test
      - store_artifacts:
          path: docs/website/public
      - persist_to_workspace:
          root: .
          paths:
            - "docs/website/public"

  docs-publish:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - setup
      - attach_workspace:
          at: .
      - run:
          name: Publish to gh-pages
          command: task ci:docs:publish

  ok-to-deploy:
    type: no-op

workflows:
  ci:
    jobs:
      # gh-pages holds only generated HTML — never run CI on it. Entry jobs (no
      # `requires`) must opt out explicitly; downstream jobs are gated by these.

      - check:
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore: gh-pages

      - test:
          matrix:
            parameters:
              executor:
                - linux
                - macos
                - windows
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore: gh-pages

      - docs:
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore: gh-pages

      - deploy:
          name: dry-run
          publish_steps:
            - run: task ci:build
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore:
                - main
                - gh-pages

      - ok-to-deploy:
          requires:
            - check
            - test
            - docs
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - release-pr:
          # One at a time, so two pushes can't race to rewrite release/next.
          serial-group: << pipeline.project.slug >>/release-pr
          requires:
            - ok-to-deploy
          context:
            - devex-release

      # Publishes only on the push that merges the release PR; halts otherwise.
      - deploy:
          serial-group: << pipeline.project.slug >>/deploy
          gate_steps:
            - run:
                name: Halt unless the release is unpublished
                command: task ci:halt-unless-unreleased
          requires:
            - ok-to-deploy
          context:
            - devex-release
            - macos-codesigning

      - docs-publish:
          serial-group: << pipeline.project.slug >>/docs-publish
          requires:
            - ok-to-deploy
          context:
            - devex-release

      - smoke-test:
          name: smoke-test-snap
          executor: linux
          install-steps:
            - run:
                name: Install snapd
                command: sudo apt update --yes && sudo apt install snapd --yes
            - run:
                name: Install circleci via Snap stable channel
                # /snap/bin has to be prepended, not just present: the machine
                # image ships its own circleci in /usr/local/bin, which would
                # otherwise shadow the snap and make this job verify the build
                # agent's CLI instead of the release.
                command: |
                  sudo snap install circleci
                  echo 'export PATH="/snap/bin:$PATH"' >> "$BASH_ENV"
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - smoke-test:
          name: smoke-test-brew
          executor: macos
          install-steps:
            - run:
                name: Install circleci via Homebrew preview tap
                command: |
                  brew update
                  rm -f /opt/homebrew/bin/circleci
                  brew install circleci-public/circleci/circleci@next
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - smoke-test-docker:
          matrix:
            parameters:
              executor:
                - linux
                - linux-arm
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - smoke-test:
          name: smoke-test-choco
          executor: windows
          install-steps:
            - run:
                name: Install circleci via Chocolatey
                command: choco install circleci-cli -y
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

Inspect a job's details, output and artifacts

## Usage

`circleci job <command> [flags]`

## Targeted Commands

| Command          | Description                            |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `artifact`       | List or download artifacts for a job   |
| `get`            | Get job details                        |
| `open`           | Open job in browser                    |
| `output`         | Work with job step output              |
| `resource-usage` | Work with a job's CPU and memory usage |

## Flags

Global flags: `-c, --config`, `--debug`, `--no-color`, `-q, --quiet` — see `circleci --help`.

## Details

Work with CircleCI jobs.

Jobs are the individual units of work within a workflow.
[exit code: 0]

toolCalls.output:
Work with a job's CPU and memory usage

## Usage

`circleci job resource-usage <command> [flags]`

## Available Commands

| Command | Description                        |
| ------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `get`   | Chart a job's CPU and memory usage |

## Flags

Global flags: `-c, --config`, `--debug`, `--no-color`, `-q, --quiet` — see `circleci --help`.

## Details

Inspect how much of its executor a job actually used.

CPU and memory are sampled at a fixed interval for the length of each
parallel execution, and reported against the limits of the resource class
the job ran on — so a job that needs a smaller (or larger) executor shows
it.
[exit code: 0]

toolCalls.name: circleci
toolCalls.output:
List recent runs for a project

## Usage

`circleci run list [flags]`

Aliases: `circleci run ls`

## Flags

| Flag                   | Description                                                                       |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-b, --branch string`  | Filter by branch                                                                  |
| `-B, --current-branch` | Filter by the currently checked-out branch                                        |
| `--jq string`          | Process values from the response using jq syntax (see `circleci help formatting`) |
| `--json`               | Output as JSON                                                                    |
| `--limit int`          | Maximum number of runs to show [default: 10] (default 10)                         |
| `--project string`     | Project slug (e.g. gh/org/repo); defaults to git remote                           |
| `--status string`      | filter by run status, e.g. success or failed                                      |

Global flags: `-c, --config`, `--debug`, `--no-color`, `-q, --quiet` — see `circleci --help`.

## Examples

- List recent runs for the current project: 
  `circleci run list`
- Filter to the branch you have checked out: 
  `circleci run list --current-branch`
- Filter to a specific branch: 
  `circleci run list --branch main`
- List runs for an explicit project: 
  `circleci run list --project gh/org/repo`
- Show the last successful run: 
  `circleci run list --status success --limit 1`
- Output as JSON for scripting: 
  `circleci run list --json`

## Details

List recent runs for a CircleCI project.

A run is one execution of a pipeline. The project is inferred from the
current git repository's remote unless overridden with --project.

JSON fields: id, phase, outcome, current_outcome, branch, tag, revision, repository_url, commit.subject/url/author_name/author_login, created_at, warnings[].type/message/description/url
[exit code: 0]

toolCalls.name: circleci
toolCalls.output:
Chart a job's CPU and memory usage

## Usage

`circleci job resource-usage get <job-id> [flags]`

## Arguments

`<job-id>` is the UUID of the job whose usage to fetch. Job UUIDs are
shown in the output of `circleci workflow get` and `circleci job get`.

## Flags

| Flag              | Description                                                                           |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--chart string`  | Plot parallel executions together or apart: auto\|combined\|separate (default "auto") |
| `--execution int` | Parallel execution index to report on (default all) (default -1)                      |
| `--jq string`     | Process values from the response using jq syntax (see `circleci help formatting`)     |
| `--json`          | Output as JSON                                                                        |

Global flags: `-c, --config`, `--debug`, `--no-color`, `-q, --quiet` — see `circleci --help`.

## Examples

- Chart a job's CPU and memory usage: 
  `circleci job resource-usage get 0dc4d8df-8f7e-41b0-a3ef-88066a5465c1`
- One chart per execution, however few there are: 
  `circleci job resource-usage get 0dc4d8df-8f7e-41b0-a3ef-88066a5465c1 --chart separate`
- Only the third parallel execution: 
  `circleci job resource-usage get 0dc4d8df-8f7e-41b0-a3ef-88066a5465c1 --execution 2`
- How close each execution came to its memory limit: 
  `circleci job resource-usage get 0dc4d8df-8f7e-41b0-a3ef-88066a5465c1 --json | jq '.executions[].memory.peak_percent_of_limit'`

## Details

Chart how much CPU and memory a job used against its resource class limits.
Peak of limit sizes the executor: under 50% on both means a smaller class fits.
Parallel executions are overlaid in color, or charted apart past 5 (--chart).

JSON fields: id, resource_class.name/cpu_count/memory_limit_bytes, executions[].execution/interval_ms/samples/duration_seconds/cpu_cores/memory_bytes/network_rx_bytes/network_tx_bytes/cpu.min/mean/max/peak_percent_of_limit (and memory.*)
[exit code: 0]

toolCalls.name: circleci
toolCalls.output:
Get a run's status

## Usage

`circleci run get [<run-id>] [flags]`

## Arguments

`<run-id>` is optional and is the UUID of the run to look up. When
omitted, the latest run is resolved from the project and branch
inferred from the current git repository's remote and checked-out
branch (override with `--project` and `--branch`). With
`--project` set, the branch defaults to main unless `--branch` is given.

## Flags

| Flag                  | Description                                                                       |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-b, --branch string` | Branch name (defaults to the current branch, or main when --project is set)       |
| `--failure-report`    | Print condensed output for every failed step; intended for agent consumption      |
| `--jq string`         | Process values from the response using jq syntax (see `circleci help formatting`) |
| `--json`              | Output as JSON                                                                    |
| `-m, --mine`          | Filter to runs owned by you.                                                      |
| `--no-interactive`    | Skip the interactive picker and resolve the latest run directly                   |
| `--project string`    | Project slug (e.g. gh/org/repo); used for latest-run lookup                       |

Global flags: `-c, --config`, `--debug`, `--no-color`, `-q, --quiet` — see `circleci --help`.

## Examples

- Get the latest run for the current branch: 
  `circleci run get`
- Get a run by UUID: 
  `circleci run get 5034460f-c7c4-4c43-9457-de07e2029e7b`
- Output as JSON for scripting: 
  `circleci run get --json`
- Get only your runs: 
  `circleci run get --mine`
- Skip the picker and resolve the latest run directly: 
  `circleci run get --no-interactive`

## Details

Display the status of a CircleCI run and its workflows.

With no run UUID in an interactive terminal, a picker walks you through the
recent runs; --no-interactive, --json, or a non-interactive session skips it
and resolves the latest run directly.

JSON fields: id, phase, outcome, current_outcome, branch, tag, revision, repository_url,
commit.subject/url/author_name/author_login, created_at, errors[].type/message,
warnings[].type/message/description/url, workflows[].id/name/phase/outcome/current_outcome/duration/
jobs[].id/name/phase/outcome/current_outcome/type
[exit code: 0]

assistantText: Now let me pull CPU/memory usage for every build job in this run.
The latest run had no usage samples for three jobs. I'll check an earlier main run for those, and to see whether the numbers hold up across runs.

I compared CPU and memory usage against each job's resource class limits for the two most recent successful `main` runs (`2f7e0fe6…` and `83581514…`). The CLI's rule of thumb is that a job using less than 50% of both its CPU and memory limits would fit on a smaller class.

**Yes: three jobs on the 4 vCPU / 16 GB `large.gen3` class (the `linux` executor) use very little of it.**

| Job | Class | Peak CPU | Peak memory | Too big? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `release-pr` | large.gen3 | 6.3% / 6.1% | 6.5% / 6.6% | **Yes, by a lot** |
| `smoke-test-snap` | large.gen3 | 14.0% / 12.1% | 6.0% / 5.8% | **Yes** |
| `docs` | large.gen3 | 28.9% / 21.6% | 9.8% / 9.6% | **Yes** |
| `check` | large.gen3 | 50.5% / 61.3% | 12.7% / 9.4% | No, CPU peaks above 50% |
| `test-linux` | large.gen3 | 84.7% | 16.6% | No |
| `test-windows` | windows.medium | 100% | 30.0% | No |
| `smoke-test-docker-linux-arm` | arm.medium | 57.6% | 11.5% | No |
| `smoke-test-choco` | windows.medium | 4.5% / 4.2% | 14.8% / 15.2% | Uses little, but probably can't go smaller (see below) |
